newsitem.title: INDIA: Key India state ends first phase of election.
newsitem.headline: Key India state ends first phase of election.

text.p: India's Uttar Pradesh state ended the first phase of crucial local elections with largely peaceful voting on Monday marred by an indifferent turnout in many places.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported sporadic violence in India's most populous state that borders Tibet and Nepal.
"There is a marked voter fatigue," communist candidate Daulat Ram told Reuters in Kanpur, the state's industrial hub, some 120 km (75 miles) from the state capital of Lucknow.
"People are beginning to look tired with the election."
Candidates said a strict police vigil that gave the bustling city a curfew-bound look deterred voters from coming out. Election officials estimated the overall turnout at 55 to 60 percent.
The three-phase local elections from Monday are expected to determine the future of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's alliance with the Congress party.
In the assembly polls, Deve Gowda's fractious United Front alliance takes on the Congress, which supports his minority government in Delhi, and the BJP in a triangular fight.

Deve Gowda's centre-left alliance gets make-or-break support from the Congress but the two are fighting against each other in the politically crucial state which has given India nine of its 12 prime ministers.
Tens of thousands of paramilitary troops have been deployed to guard the election in the violence-prone state of 140 million.
Polling for 135 seats took place on Monday. Remaining polls for the 425-member assembly will be held on October 3 and 7.

Police eased a round-the-clock curfew in the Moslem majority quarters of Lucknow, the state capital once ruled by colourful Moslem Shi'ite nawabs of Oudh, but now the main base of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP),
"These polls were among the best held," a police official told Reuters.
In Kanpur, once a communist bastion, paramilitary forces from the northern state of Punjab stopped all traffic, checked vehicles and generally kept a tight vigil.
The city saw massive anti-Sikh violence in 1984 in revenge for the assassination of then prime minister Indira Gandhi by two Sikh bodyguards.

The BJP's campaign to build a Hindu temple at the site of a disputed 16th century mosque in Ayodhya triggered a vicious cycle of Hindu-Moslem riots between 1990 and 1993 that killed more than 3,000 people.
While the BJP is playing down the issue in its campaign, the government, taking no chances, has staggered the polls over three days to cover the three disputed sites on different days.
Scores of people were injured as Hindu and Moslem groups clashed last week over the erection of a Hindu idol in Lucknow.

Uttar Pradesh, which is more populous than Japan or Pakistan, sends 85 deputies to the 545-member federal parliament, where the BJP is the biggest single party. Analysts say the state, once a bastion of the Congress party which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947, could help a recent trend of coalition politics.
